explanations: luna: The section's painted surface looks as if it contains a woven inner pattern; these people say they believe in God and the Last Day while the ayah says they are not believers, a specific claim-versus-reality split. | terra: People say they believe in God and the Last Day while they are not believers, a concise verbal surface over a contrary interior.
luna: This next ayah says they think they deceive God and believers but deceive only themselves; it makes the apparent surface and hidden reality in 2:8 explicit.
luna: The next ayah names disease in their hearts and says they lie (يَكْذِبُونَ); it connects inner condition to the section's root for a lie expressed in one's state.
terra: When confronted over corruption they call themselves reformers, making their description of their acts contradict the acts themselves.
terra: God identifies them as the actual corrupters, supplying the judgment beneath their self-painted label in 2:11.

luna: They tell believers they believe, then privately say they were only mocking; this is a specific outward claim and concealed stance like the section's false surface. | terra: They say “We believe” before believers and reverse themselves when alone with their leaders; their profession changes with the watching audience.
luna: The preceding parable says a fire briefly lights the surroundings and then God takes away its light; that exposed, temporary appearance introduces the intermittence completed by 2:20.

luna: This ayah sets the second parable in a storm with darkness, thunder and lightning; the next ayah's walking-then-stopping is its own added detail and the specific link to the source's interrupted motion.

luna: These people walk when lightning gives light and stop when darkness returns; that exact start-and-halt movement parallels the source's animal that runs one stretch then stops and its prayer abandoned when no one watches. | terra: In the hypocrites' storm-parable they walk whenever lightning gives light and stand still when darkness returns; their movement advances only while conditions please the eye.

luna: The command not to mix truth with falsehood or conceal truth (لَا تَلْبِسُوا الْحَقَّ بِالْبَاطِلِ) gives a verbal counterpart to the source's surface that appears to contain a pattern it does not.

luna: The question “Do you command righteousness and forget yourselves?” names speech whose own conduct fails it, the same action-level falsehood developed from the source's root ك ذ ب. | terra: Those who order righteousness while forgetting themselves recite the Book yet fail to carry its command into their own action, a direct saying-doing split.
terra: Prayer is burdensome except for the inwardly humble, so the same visible act is distinguished by the disposition that inhabits it.

luna: This ayah describes people who write a text with their own hands and claim it is from God for a price; the counterfeit object and its false claim directly echo the source's fabricated-looking cloth and lie-in-action root.
terra: صِبْغَةَ ٱللَّهِ names God's “coloring” and joins it to worship; it offers a transforming coloration of allegiance against the source's dye that merely imitates woven truth.
terra: The change of prayer-direction distinguishes who follows the Messenger from who turns on his heels; a visible alteration tests whether allegiance continues.

luna: The ayah says some conceal what God revealed and sell it for a small price; it adds the specific deed of hiding truth behind an outward transaction, which the source's inner-intention image makes perceptible.

luna: The section sets the root ك ذ ب against truth and says deeds expose a false surface; this ayah says turning one's face is not righteousness, then names giving, prayer and patience as the deeds of those who are truthful (صَدَقُوا). | terra: Righteousness is not the visible turning of faces; care for orphans and the needy, prayer, almsgiving, fidelity, and endurance make people ٱلَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا۟, the actionally truthful opposite of the painted life.
terra: A man's speech about worldly life impresses the listener and he invokes God over his heart, yet the ayah says his hidden reality is fierce hostility.
terra: When he turns away, he destroys crops and offspring; conduct after the impressive speech of 2:204 exposes what its polished surface concealed.
terra: When told to fear God, pride carries him further into sin; the response to correction confirms that the attractive statement in 2:204 was unsupported within.
terra: In the treatment of orphans, God knows the corrupter from the reformer even when both can share a household; the same outward arrangement is judged by conduct and intent.

luna: The source's dictionary form دَانَ يَدينُ leaves the oath-taker to his intention; this ayah likewise distinguishes unintentional oaths from what hearts have earned, locating judgment beneath the words. | terra: God does not take people to account for idle wording in oaths but for what their hearts earn, closely matching the source dictionary sense of holding the swearer to inward intention.

luna: The command to guard the prayers (حَافِظُوا عَلَى الصَّلَوَاتِ) is a direct opposite to being away from prayer or stopping when unobserved. | terra: Guarding the prayers and standing devoutly describes attention and preservation, directly opposed to distance from prayer despite performing its pieces.

luna: This ayah describes spending without following it with reminders or injury, showing how the act must continue in conduct after the visible gift; that is the section's test of whether the apparent good is real. | terra: Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminder or injury let the good act retain its promised continuation.

luna: A kind word and pardon are called better than charity followed by injury; this gives a precise boundary for the section's claim that visible giving can be contradicted by what follows. | terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, because a later act can expose and cancel the apparent goodness of the first.

luna: The source's dictionary form كذّابة is a dyed surface that looks embroidered without woven stitches; here rain strips soil from the rock, exposing the attractive cover as unsupported. | terra: Showy spending, رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ, is soil spread over rock: rain exposes the stone beneath, exactly as the section's apparent weave is exposed as surface paint.

luna: After the rock whose soil washes away in 2:264, this adjacent parable shows a garden rooted on high ground yielding fruit; it contrasts a surface coating with growth that has a real root. | terra: Spending from desire for God's pleasure and inward firmness is a garden that yields under rain; it is the fertile counter-scene to the soil-coated rock of 2:264.
terra: A fruitful garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and dependent, staging a promising provision whose later failure discloses the need for durable deeds.
luna: The command not to choose inferior things for charity, which one would accept only with closed eyes, directly tests whether a gift's apparent value matches its substance.
luna: The source's dictionary sense of د ي ن leaves the oath-taker to intent; this ayah says God knows what people spend and vow, connecting intention to accountable acts.

luna: This ayah says charity given openly or kept hidden is known to God and that hidden giving is better; it distinguishes an audience-facing display from the inner intention emphasized in the section. | terra: Public charity can be good while concealed charity to the poor is better; the ayah supplies a boundary showing that visibility itself is not hypocrisy, while motive and recipient still matter.

luna: The needy are restrained from asking and appear self-sufficient, yet their need can be recognized by their marks; this is a specific reversal in which outward appearance hides the real condition.

luna: This ayah describes spending by night and day, secretly and openly, with reward from God; sustained giving whose worth is not confined to spectators reverses the section's show. | terra: Spending by night and day, secretly and publicly, depicts giving that continues across time and audience instead of stopping when eyes turn away.
luna: This repeated command asks why truth is mixed with falsehood and knowingly concealed; it independently restates the hidden-under-cover relation of the painted cloth.
luna: Some people twist their tongues with scripture so listeners think their words come from the Book, though they do not; this is a specific verbal surface that imitates a real underlying pattern.
luna: The ayah says righteousness is not attained until one spends what one loves; the real cost of a gift tests the inner commitment behind its visible appearance.
terra: Hatred has already appeared from opponents' mouths while what their breasts conceal is greater, distinguishing the visible leakage from the deeper interior.
terra: They say “We believe” when they meet believers but bite their fingertips in rage when alone, changing their visible posture with the audience.
terra: The question whether people will turn on their heels if the Messenger dies tests whether the professed course continues after its visible leader is gone.
terra: The fighters initially rout the enemy, then lose resolve, dispute, and disobey after seeing what they desire; the assault breaks where the gaze finds its reward.
terra: The would-be fighters say with their mouths what is not in their hearts; their refusal to follow into battle makes speech, interior, and movement diverge.

luna: This ayah recalls a covenant to make scripture clear rather than conceal it, then says they cast it aside and sold it cheaply; it gives a concrete broken obligation next to the praise-for-unearned-credit detail in 3:188.

luna: Those who love praise for what they did not do are named alongside rejoicing in what they did; the gap between public credit and actual deed directly fits the section's false surface. | terra: People rejoice in what they have done and love praise for what they did not do; the desired public image is explicitly detached from the deed beneath it.

luna: This ayah says those who unjustly consume orphan property are consuming fire; it gives a specific harmful act toward the orphan that confirms the section's claim that the denial is exposed in conduct.

luna: The command to do good to orphans and the needy gives the positive action against the section's orphan-pushing and failure to encourage food for the poor. | terra: Worship without association is immediately joined to good treatment of orphans and the needy, while proud display is rejected; inner allegiance and social action form one fabric.

luna: This ayah joins miserliness to urging others to be miserly and concealing God's bounty; that is a specific opposite of the section's expected giving and its exposed inner state. | terra: The proud are characterized by miserliness, urging others to be miserly, and concealing God's bounty, the social conduct beneath the posture condemned in 4:36.

luna: The source's root ر ء ي includes public showing; this ayah describes spending “to be seen by people” (رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ) while lacking belief in God and the Last Day, joining display to denied dīn. | terra: Those who spend to be seen by people and do not believe in God or the Last Day make ostentatious giving the visible form of denied judgment.
terra: Those intoxicated may not approach prayer until they know what they are saying; the ayah draws a boundary between bodily performance and conscious presence within it.
terra: People who declare themselves pure are corrected by God's prerogative to purify; outward self-description cannot establish the inward state.
terra: A person among the community deliberately lags behind, giving a Quranic bodily scene for the source dictionary's slowing or delaying step.
terra: If success comes, the laggard wishes he had been present for the gain; his movement follows the audience and outcome rather than a stable commitment.

luna: This ayah combines rising lazily for prayer with “showing people” (يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ) and little remembrance; it makes the section's prayer-away and public surface explicit. | terra: The hypocrites rise to prayer lazily and only to be seen by people; prayer has its visible posture while its attention remains with the spectators.
luna: The hypocrites are described as wavering between two sides (مُّذَبْذَبِينَ); this names an unstable, unfinished stance, a specific boundary against the section's faithful continuation.
terra: Moses commands his people to enter the holy land and not turn on their backs, a direct movement boundary for the source dictionary's advance that either holds or fails.
terra: Some say “We believe” with their mouths though their hearts have not believed, an exact statement of the section's surface-and-interior split.

luna: The source's dictionary form about an oath-taker turns on intention; this ayah distinguishes careless oaths from deliberate ones (عَقَّدتُّمُ الْأَيْمَانَ), giving the same word-versus-intent boundary in its own context. | terra: Idle oaths are distinguished from oaths deliberately bound; judgment passes beneath spoken form to the commitment actually made.
terra: Marked livestock customs are denied divine sanction and called a lie fabricated against God; an animal's visible status has been made to counterfeit religion.

luna: This repeated command says not to repel those who call on God morning and evening, seeking His face; it gives another specific reversal of the orphan-pushing image and contrasts devotion with audience-facing display. | terra: The Prophet must not drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening seeking His face; their sustained, inwardly directed worship outweighs social appearance.

luna: People make scripture into sheets, displaying some and concealing much; this specific selective covering resembles the source's surface pattern that gives an incomplete account of what lies beneath.
terra: Invented rules mark crops and livestock as restricted and even suppress God's name over animals; visible animal categories are made to carry a fabricated religious claim.
terra: They make what is inside livestock bellies lawful for men and forbidden to wives, with another rule if it is stillborn; hidden animal contents become material for false religious distinctions.
terra: Those who prohibit God's provision through invention are declared lost and unguided, giving the judgment on the animal-and-womb fabrications in 6:138-139.

terra: The parallel question about male, female, and what wombs contain demands knowledge “if you are truthful,” preparing the camel version in 6:144 and testing religious claims against concealed fact.
terra: The ayah names camels, asks what the females' wombs contain, and ends by condemning a lie attributed to God; camel, hidden pregnancy, and religious falsehood meet in one scene.

luna: This ayah pairs careful treatment of an orphan's property with full, just measure; it is a concrete boundary against the section's displaced care and the shortfall that makes an outward exchange false.
terra: The speaker declares prayer, sacrifice, life, and death all for God, placing visible worship inside a single undivided orientation.
terra: Literal clothing and adornment are acknowledged, but the garment of reverence is better; the ayah marks the boundary between an attractive surface and the inward clothing that carries value.
luna: Shu'ayb's people are told to give full measure and weight and not deprive others; that explicit fair-exchange boundary reverses the source's root ك ذ ب as a lie enacted in behavior.
terra: A pregnancy begins as a light burden and later grows heavy and manifest; the womb's developing condition supplies the truthful bodily disclosure named in the source dictionary.
terra: After receiving the sound child for which they prayed, they assign partners regarding the gift; the response fails to continue the intention voiced during pregnancy.
terra: True believers' hearts tremble at God's mention and their faith increases when revelation is recited, locating profession in an inward response that continues to grow.
terra: They establish prayer and spend from their provision, joining worship to material care rather than leaving prayer as a surface pattern.
terra: أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ حَقًّا makes the inward response and acts of 8:2-3 the evidence that belief is real.
terra: Believers meeting an advancing force are forbidden to turn their backs, directly marking the boundary at which a charge would become the section's failed assault.
terra: Turning away is allowed only for a maneuver or regrouping; the ayah distinguishes purposeful continued combat from simple retreat.

luna: This ayah calls the disbelievers' worship at the Sacred House whistling and clapping; it is a specific outward religious performance whose substance does not match the name, unlike real prayer. | terra: Their “prayer” at the House is only whistling and clapping, a visible performance bearing the name of prayer without its inward substance.
terra: When meeting a force, believers are commanded to stand firm and remember God, the sustained battlefield stance opposed to an attack that stops before its deed is done.
terra: They must not dispute and lose courage, but remain patient; inward cohesion preserves the outward advance begun in 8:45.

luna: The ayah describes people going out boastfully and showing off to others (رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ); this is a concrete public display corresponding to the source's root ر ء ي and its audience-facing appearance. | terra: The fighters leave home boastfully and رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ; even a public march can orient itself toward watchers rather than its professed end.
terra: Satan adorns the fighters' deeds and promises protection, then turns on his heels when the armies meet; attractive assurance terminates in literal battlefield retreat.
terra: At Hunayn impressive numbers avail nothing and the fighters turn away fleeing; visible strength fails at the moment the charge should continue.
terra: When summoned to go forth, people become heavy and cling to the earth; the command begins a course that their slowed bodies refuse to continue.
terra: They would follow if gain were near and the journey easy, then swear they could have gone; the unmade journey exposes the oath, and God calls them liars.
terra: Had they truly intended to go out, they would have prepared for it; absent preparation makes inward intention legible through action.
luna: This ayah says their prayer is approached lazily and their spending reluctantly; those half-present acts give a direct counterpart to the section's interrupted prayer and failed giving.
luna: This ayah says hypocritical men and women close their hands, command evil and forbid good; its withheld hand gives the section's denial a specific material action.

luna: The source's idioms describe a beginning that promises continuation but does not hold; this adjacent ayah introduces a pledge to give charity if bounty comes, whose reversal follows. | terra: They covenant that if God gives bounty they will donate and become righteous, establishing the beginning whose promise the following ayat test.

luna: After the pledge in 9:75, this ayah says that when bounty came they became miserly and turned away; the beginning does not hold through to the promised act. | terra: Once bounty arrives they withhold it and turn away, so continuation disproves the posture taken at the beginning of their vow.

luna: The source explicitly says ك ذ ب can describe conduct, not only speech; this ayah links breaking their promise to hypocrisy and says they used to lie (يَكْذِبُونَ), naming both the failed deed and falsehood. | terra: Their hypocrisy is tied to breaking the promise and lying, بِمَآ أَخْلَفُوا۟ ... وَبِمَا كَانُوا۟ يَكْذِبُونَ; the failed continuation becomes an inward condition.
terra: People are commanded to act because God, the Messenger, and believers will see their deeds, and God will disclose them; the decisive gaze remains when the performer's chosen audience does not.
terra: A mosque is built for harm and division while its builders swear they intended only good; the sacred exterior is paint over a contrary intention, and God calls them liars.
terra: The Prophet is told not to stand in that mosque and is directed to one founded on reverence, distinguishing two outwardly similar structures by their foundation and intent.
terra: A building founded on reverence is set against one on a collapsing bank that falls into fire; what lies beneath the visible building determines whether it stands.
terra: In danger at sea people call on God with sincere religion and promise gratitude if rescued, establishing an inward profession whose continuation will immediately be tested.
terra: Once rescued they transgress on earth, so the safe continuation contradicts the sincere crisis-prayer and promise of 10:22.

luna: The earth's growth first adorns itself, then is cut down as though it had not flourished; the specific change from attractive surface to absence echoes the source's false appearance and stopped motion. | terra: The world's vegetation becomes adorned until its owners think they control it, then is cut down as if it never flourished; an impressive beginning fails its implied promise of duration.
terra: People turn God's provision into “lawful” and “unlawful”; the question asks whether God permitted it or they fabricate a lie against Him.
terra: Noah refuses to drive away the believers who will meet their Lord; social appearance cannot justify repelling people whose inward account belongs to God.
luna: This ayah commands full measure and weight and forbids depriving people of their due; it is another direct boundary for dishonest outward dealing.

terra: Joseph's brothers report that they went racing and that a wolf ate him, adding that Jacob would not believe them though they were “truthful”; the rehearsed speech precedes the lying shirt in 12:18.
terra: Joseph's brothers bring false blood on a shirt, دَمٍ كَذِبٍ; a piece of cloth literally carries a lie in its visible condition, closely matching the section's painted fabric.
terra: The proposed test makes the shirt's physical state adjudicate two spoken claims: a front tear would make her truthful and him a liar, so cloth can disclose rather than counterfeit truth.
terra: A tear from behind would make her the liar and Joseph truthful; this reverses the section's lying textile by letting a garment's condition expose the speaker.
terra: When the rear tear is actually seen, the surface evidence defeats the fabricated story; visible cloth here reveals what lies underneath the words.
terra: God knows what every female bears and what wombs diminish or increase, placing hidden pregnancy and changing measure within exact knowledge rather than visual inference.
terra: Those who fulfill God's covenant and do not break the pledge model a beginning whose continuation keeps faith with it.

luna: This ayah pairs prayer and spending, done privately and publicly, with seeking God's face and repelling evil with good; the explicit intention and continuing response clarify what a merely displayed act lacks. | terra: Those who endure seeking God's face, establish prayer, and spend secretly and publicly embody acts held together by inward aim across changing audiences.
terra: Those who break God's covenant after confirming it show precisely how a solemn beginning can be contradicted by what follows.
terra: The disbelievers' deeds are ashes scattered by a violent wind, so an apparent accumulation proves unable to endure or deliver what it seemed to promise.
terra: A good word is a good tree with a firm root, making truth an inwardly grounded form rather than decoration laid on a surface.
terra: The rooted tree gives fruit repeatedly by its Lord's permission; its continuing yield shows that the promising exterior is supported within.
terra: A bad word is an uprooted tree with no stability, an outward form unable to stand because nothing beneath secures it.
terra: Livestock yield pure, palatable milk from within between waste and blood; what is hidden inside truly provides what the drink's appearance promises.
terra: The command to fulfill God's covenant and not break confirmed oaths states the durable course that the unraveling-yarn image in 16:92 explains.

luna: The section's deceptive cloth only looks woven; this ayah warns against a woman who unspins her yarn after making it strong (نَقَضَتْ غَزْلَهَا), a contrary textile image of an actual construction undone after a pledge. | terra: The woman who unravels her yarn after spinning it strong turns a textile into the image of oaths used deceitfully; the finished surface and the promised continuation both come apart.
terra: Oaths must not become deception lest a firmly planted foot slip; inner fraud turns an apparently settled step into interrupted movement.
terra: “What is with you runs out, and what is with God remains” states the lasting-versus-failing measure implicit in milk that ceases and an act that stops midway.
terra: A secure town with abundant provision denies God's favors and is made to taste the garment of hunger and fear because of its deeds; outward plenty becomes a garment matching inner conduct.
terra: A messenger came with clear signs, but the town denied him and punishment seized it, identifying the تكذيب beneath the changed garment of 16:112.
terra: Tongues falsely label things lawful and unlawful and thereby fabricate a lie against God; religious judgment becomes a verbal surface unsupported by divine warrant.
luna: The command to give full measure and weigh with a straight balance sets a specific standard for an exchange whose appearance must match what is actually delivered.
terra: The earth's adornment is explicitly a test of who is best in deed, so visible beauty is judged by conduct rather than taken as its own truth.
terra: God will make that adorned surface barren ground, exposing the temporary status of the pattern described in 18:7.

luna: The ayah commands the Prophet not to drive away people who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face; it directly reverses pushing the vulnerable away and makes intention, rather than public adornment, the measure. | terra: He must remain with those who call on their Lord seeking His face and not let his eyes pass beyond them toward worldly adornment; gaze is subordinated to sincere persistence.
terra: Vegetation mingles after rain and then becomes dry fragments scattered by wind; flourishing appearance does not keep its implied promise to remain.
luna: Wealth and children are called the adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better; this gives the source's painted adornment a specific contrast with what truly remains.
terra: The question offers to identify the greatest losers in deeds, directing attention from self-description to what action finally amounts to.

luna: These are people whose effort is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well; the explicit misreading of their own performance parallels a life whose surface looks right but does not hold. | terra: Their effort is lost while they think they are doing beautiful work; the perceived pattern of a life does not match the fabric of its result.
terra: One who hopes to meet the Lord must do righteous work and associate no one in worship, joining outward deed to an undivided addressee rather than a human audience.
terra: Later generations neglect prayer and follow desires; the verse depicts being carried away from prayer as a life-course, rather than a forgotten detail inside one performance.
terra: The Prophet must not extend his eyes toward the flower of worldly life, a temporary test; the ayah disciplines the gaze and names God's provision as better and more lasting.
terra: The command to establish prayer in one's household and persist patiently in it, وَٱصْطَبِرْ عَلَيْهَا, supplies the durable prayer immediately after the warning against eye-catching display.
terra: One worships God on an edge, staying for benefit and turning back under trial; conditional worship is precisely a motion that begins but will not carry through.
terra: Sacrificial flesh and blood do not reach God, while reverence does; the ayah expressly separates visible ritual material from the inward reality that gives it value.

luna: The section stresses being “away from” prayer (عن) while appearing to pray; this ayah places humility “in” prayer (فِي صَلَاتِهِمْ), a direct boundary between the two stances. | terra: The faithful are humble فِى صَلَاتِهِمْ, inwardly present within their prayer; that exact construction clarifies the section's contrast with being heedless عَن prayer.
terra: The inwardly humble worshippers of the passage are active in almsgiving, carrying prayer into material responsibility toward others.
terra: They faithfully keep trusts and covenants before 23:9 returns to guarded prayer, so the worship is enclosed by durable conduct.

luna: After describing humility in prayer in 23:2, this ayah says the believers guard their prayers; it adds continued care to the inward presence contrasted with the section's inattention. | terra: The believers guard their prayers, repeating within al-Mu'minun the durable opposite of heedlessness from prayer.
terra: Livestock provide drink from what is in their bellies and many other benefits; the Quranic animal genuinely supplies from within what its condition offers outwardly.

luna: This ayah forbids those with bounty to swear that they will stop giving to relatives, needy people and migrants; it directly addresses a beginning-to-stop gift and commands its continuation and forgiveness.
luna: This ayah says tongues, hands and feet will testify to what people did; it repeats the specific image of bodily action disclosing what a person might wish to conceal.

luna: Trade does not distract these men from God's remembrance, prayer and almsgiving; the ayah supplies sustained worship and giving as a direct opposite to prayer abandoned when unobserved. | terra: Neither trade nor sale distracts these people from remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving; the visible attraction that breaks the gathering in 62:11 cannot stop their course.

luna: The deeds of disbelievers are likened to a mirage that looks like water but yields nothing when reached; this is a precise Qur'anic surface that promises substance but has none, like the source's painted cloth. | terra: The unbelievers' deeds are a mirage the thirsty person counts as water until arrival reveals nothing and God's account; visible promise, failed continuation, and judgment meet exactly.

luna: The next likeness is layered sea darkness in which even a hand is hard to see; it supplies the converse of the cloth's deceptive visibility, showing the hidden reality after 24:39's false appearance.
terra: They say “We believe and obey,” then a group turns away; the second movement exposes the first statement as a surface claim.
terra: When summoned to God's and the Messenger's judgment, a group refuses, showing concretely that the announced obedience in 24:47 never entered conduct.
terra: They swear their strongest oaths that they would go out if commanded, but are told not to swear and that known obedience is required; deeds, not emphatic surface speech, are the test.
terra: “I am not one to drive away the believers” repeats the boundary against judging and repelling the socially weak by their visible status.
luna: The people are told to give full measure and not be among those who defraud; this is a direct reversal of a life that lies through its actions.
luna: The next ayah says to weigh with a straight balance; it supplies the concrete measure standard following 26:181.
luna: This ayah forbids depriving people of their due or spreading corruption; it completes the fair-measure warning with the actual harm that a false exchange causes.

luna: This ayah asks whether people think they can merely say “we believe” and be left untested; it raises the difference between a surface claim and a life whose truth is shown in the next ayah. | terra: People are not left merely to say “We believe”; the claim must pass through a continuing test rather than remain a verbal pattern.

luna: The next ayah says God tests people to distinguish the truthful from the liars; the source's root ك ذ ب similarly treats truth or falsehood as something manifested beyond a spoken claim. | terra: Testing makes the truthful and the liars known, so time and continued action disclose what the initial profession contained.
terra: One says “We believe,” treats human persecution like God's punishment, then claims fellowship when victory comes; affiliation shifts with the visible audience and outcome.

luna: This ayah says prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing; it connects the section's visible prayer movements to the conduct that should follow from prayer. | terra: Prayer is said to restrain indecency and wrongdoing; its continuing effect in life distinguishes an inwardly operative prayer from a display confined to its postures.
terra: Ship passengers call on God with sincere religion, then associate partners once brought ashore; one ayah contains both the inward-sounding beginning and its failed continuation.
terra: Only God knows what is in the wombs and what a person will earn tomorrow, marking the limit of reading hidden truth or future continuation from visible signs.
terra: Mistaken naming is excused while what hearts intend is accountable, another explicit judgment beneath outward wording.
terra: Some claim their houses are exposed although they are not and seek leave only to flee; a verbal pretext covers the intended retreat.
terra: They had already covenanted not to turn their backs, so flight would make a pledged martial beginning fail in its continuation.
terra: God knows the hinderers who summon their fellows away and come to battle only a little, making interrupted martial movement evidence of their stance.
terra: Their eyes roll in fear during danger, then their tongues become sharp when danger passes; bodily gaze and speech change with the watching circumstance, and the ayah denies their faith.

luna: The section's root ك ذ ب names a failed continuation; this ayah calls those who were true to their covenant with God (صَدَقُوا مَا عَاهَدُوا) and says some fulfilled it while others await without changing. | terra: Men who صَدَقُوا۟ مَا عَٰهَدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ عَلَيْهِ fulfill or continue waiting upon their covenant without changing, embodying the section's truthful, unbroken movement.
terra: An evil deed is made attractive so its doer sees it as good; sight reads an ornamental surface that conduct does not substantiate.

luna: The ayah describes reciting scripture, establishing prayer and spending secretly and openly while hoping for a trade that will not fail; its sustained, inwardly directed acts reverse the source's short-lived display. | terra: Those who establish prayer and spend secretly and publicly hope for a commerce that will never perish; constancy and audience-independent giving answer both the stopped prayer and failed provision.

luna: On the Day of Judgment mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to deeds; the body's own state exposes action, like the source's cloth that says nothing yet tells a lie by its condition.
terra: The command to worship God while making the religion sincere for Him places visible worship wholly inside its intended allegiance.

terra: Pure religion belongs to God, while claimed intermediaries are justified by a stated intention; God judges the dispute and does not guide the liar, testing the explanation beneath worship's surface.
terra: Rain produces crops of varied colors that then wither, yellow, and become debris, repeating the passage from eye-catching surface to exposed impermanence.

luna: Hearing, sight and skin testify against people about what they did; this directly parallels the source's claim that a person's state can tell the truth of their actions without a verbal confession.
luna: The next ayah says the people ask their own skins why they testified, and the skins answer that God made them speak; it completes the bodily-witness image begun in 41:20.
luna: This ayah says they had not hidden themselves from their own hearing, sight or skins; it makes the gap between concealment and actual exposure explicit after the testimony in 41:20–21.
terra: Those who say “Our Lord is God” and then remain steadfast make later conduct carry the promise of the initial declaration.
terra: No fruit leaves its sheath and no female conceives or gives birth outside God's knowledge; enclosed fruit and womb alike place hidden content under exact knowledge.
terra: The same sequence of declaring God as Lord and remaining steadfast repeats the section's truthful alternative to a life that starts and stops.
terra: The battle instruction continues the blow until the enemy is subdued and bonds are secured, closely matching the source dictionary's assault that does not stop before striking.
terra: Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste does not change; this is the precise enduring reversal of the source idiom in which expected milk fails and “lies.”
terra: Those who ask for a surah reveal a death-struck gaze when decisive fighting is prescribed; the requested beginning falters when action arrives.
terra: Obedience and a fitting word are named, then the ayah says truthfulness to God would be better once the matter is resolved; continuation tests the spoken posture.
terra: People turn back after guidance has become clear, making later retreat disclose that the earlier advance did not hold.
terra: Those with diseased hearts are asked whether they think God will not expose their resentments, directly announcing that the concealed layer cannot remain hidden.
terra: They could be recognized by visible marks and are already recognizable by the tone of speech, while God knows deeds; body, voice, and action disclose what lies within.
terra: A pledge to the Messenger is a pledge to God: whoever breaks it harms himself, while fulfillment carries reward; the ayah makes continuation the truth of the initial handclasp.
terra: The desert Arabs will offer a verbal excuse, saying with their tongues what is not in their hearts; absent conduct and hidden intention qualify the speech.
terra: The desert Arabs are told that faith has not entered their hearts despite their claim “We believe,” sharply separating an outward label from inward reality.
terra: True believers sustain their profession without doubt and expend themselves in action; أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلصَّٰدِقُونَ makes persevering conduct the proof of truth.

luna: The source's root س ه و distinguishes being away from prayer from being inattentive to a part within it; this ayah uses the same root for people immersed in confusion, a related heedlessness outside the prayer setting. | terra: The same adjective سَاهُونَ describes people immersed in heedlessness, supporting the section's reading of heedlessness as an encompassing distance rather than a small lapse within prayer.
terra: God knew people while they were embryos in their mothers' wombs, so they must not declare themselves pure; unseen origin and inward reverence defeat self-painted virtue before 53:33-34.

luna: The section's root ر ء ي opens with “Have you seen?” and its running image includes a movement that fails to continue; this ayah asks about the one who turned away (تَوَلَّىٰ), introducing the concrete withdrawal in its next verse. | terra: أَفَرَءَيْتَ introduces the person who turns away with the same arresting “have you seen?” stance as 107:1; 53:34 then shows what his turning away looks like in action.

luna: The source's dictionary idiom for the camel's milk is that it was expected to last but stopped; this adjacent ayah says he gave a little, then stopped (أَكْدَىٰ), making the failed continuation explicit. | terra: He gives a little and then stops, أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ, the Quranic enactment of the section's charge, milk, and run that promise continuation but break off.
luna: The same passage recalls Abraham, “the one who fulfilled” (وَفَّىٰ); this continuing example supplies the opposite of the section's start that does not carry through.
luna: The passage says a human being has only what he strives for; it gives the interrupted giving in 53:34 its measure in actual effort.
luna: The following ayah says that his striving will be seen; it connects the source's “Have you seen?” framing to deeds that are exposed and assessed.
luna: This ayah commands maintaining the balance with justice and forbids shortfall; its exact boundary against withholding a due amount fits the source's action-level falsehood.
terra: Believers are warned not to become like earlier communities whose hearts hardened as time lengthened; duration reveals whether an initial reception remains alive within.

luna: The ayah compares worldly life to growth that first pleases and adorns the earth, then yellows and breaks; its visible beauty and cessation parallel the source's appearance and interrupted continuation. | terra: Worldly growth pleases the observer, then dries, yellows, and becomes debris; what delights the eye is tested by whether it remains.

luna: This ayah says people take their oaths as a shield and turn others from God's way; a protective-looking exterior concealing contrary intent fits the section's painted covering. | terra: They take their oaths as a shield and obstruct God's way, a repeated Quranic formulation in which solemn speech becomes a concealing surface for contrary action.

luna: On the Day all are raised, the hypocrites swear to God as they swear to people and think they stand on something; the repeated false oath makes the section's word-versus-intention theme specific. | terra: Even at resurrection the hypocrites swear to God as they swore to people and imagine it helps them; the final Judge identifies the practiced oath-surface as a lie.
terra: Hypocrites promise their allies that they will leave with them and help them fight, while God testifies that they are liars; speech launches a movement their acts will not complete.
terra: The promised departure and aid will not occur, and even if they fight they will turn their backs; this is the section's failed charge spelled out as a battlefield prediction.

luna: The section says a life can lie through what it does; this ayah asks why people say what they do not do, stating that mismatch directly. | terra: The direct question “Why do you say what you do not do?” states the section's claim that lying can be the mismatch between a life's surface and its acts.

luna: This adjacent ayah calls it greatly hateful to say what one does not do; it supplies the judgment on the speech-and-action split named in 61:2. | terra: This ayah names the saying-doing mismatch as intensely hateful to God, giving the divine judgment beneath the attractive verbal surface described in 61:2.

luna: After condemning words unsupported by deeds in 61:2–3, this ayah praises people who stand together like a solid structure; the real, joined structure contrasts with the source's cloth that only looks woven. | terra: God loves fighters in a rank like a solid structure; the compact, mutually supporting formation reverses both the failed charge and the propped timbers whose stance lacks inward support.

luna: The section's painted cloth seems to carry woven content without having it; this ayah compares those entrusted with scripture but not carrying it out to a donkey carrying books, an unusually exact image of outside possession without inward realization. | terra: The donkey carrying books has the visible burden of revelation without assimilating it, like a patterned exterior unsupported by an inward weave.
terra: At the Friday call believers must hasten to remembrance and leave trade; this command defines the course that the sight of trade interrupts in 62:11.
terra: After prayer is completed people may disperse and seek God's bounty, showing that commerce has its proper place after worship rather than breaking it midway.
terra: The hypocrites utter a factually true testimony about the Messenger, yet God calls them liars because their act of witnessing does not correspond to their inner state.
terra: They make their oaths a shield, turning a visible profession into a covering that conceals obstruction.
terra: They believed and then disbelieved, so their hearts were sealed; the sequence is another beginning whose continuation contradicts it.

luna: The section's root ر ء ي includes good appearance and public showing; this ayah says their bodies please the viewer, then compares them to propped-up logs, separating display from what sustains it. | terra: Bodies that please the eye are likened to propped timber; their upright appearance comes from an external support rather than an inwardly living structure.
terra: When invited to seek forgiveness, the hypocrites turn their heads and are seen withdrawing arrogantly; their bodies disclose the stance concealed by polished appearance.
terra: They instruct others not to spend on those around the Messenger until they disperse, making withholding the social action beneath their professed affiliation.
terra: Wealth and children must not distract believers from remembrance; the ayah names the visible attractions that can pull worship off its course.
luna: This parable opens with owners of a garden who intend to harvest it; the following verses reveal their plan to withhold its crop from the poor, continuing the section's provision scene.
luna: The garden owners make no exception in their plan; this detail frames the refusal to share that becomes explicit in 68:24.
luna: They urge one another to go harvest their crop; this starts the purposeful movement whose hidden aim is revealed in the next verses as keeping the poor out.
luna: The garden owners go off whispering together before the harvest; their concealed plan begins the concrete refusal to share provision that the section marks as evidence.
luna: Their whisper is made explicit: they resolve that no poor person will enter the garden; this directly stages failure to encourage or provide food.
luna: They leave early, confident and determined to keep the harvest; this shows a sustained, purposeful action in the very direction opposite to giving.
terra: The condemned person did not believe in the supreme God; 69:34 immediately makes failure toward the poor the visible continuation of that unbelief.
terra: He did not urge feeding the needy, reproducing the surah's move from denied faith to the social act that proves it.
terra: Human beings become withholding when good reaches them; the next ayah's exception makes constancy in prayer answer this concrete refusal to give.
terra: “Except the prayerful” opens the exception to anxious withholding, and 70:23 defines them by continual prayer.

luna: Against the source's prayer performed only while watched, this ayah describes people who remain constant (دَائِمُونَ) in prayer; the continuity is the opposite of stopping when the audience leaves. | terra: Those who remain constant in prayer, دَآئِمُونَ, are the explicit opposite of a prayer-run that stops when the watcher disappears.

luna: This ayah specifies a known right in wealth for the asker and deprived person, placing material provision immediately after the constant prayer in 70:23. | terra: Those constant in prayer also recognize a fixed share in their wealth, showing prayer continued into material responsibility.

luna: This adjacent ayah names the asker and deprived person as the holders of that right, making the section's concern with feeding and withholding concrete. | terra: That recognized share belongs to the petitioner and deprived, completing the contrast with prayer accompanied by withholding small aid.
terra: The same people keep trusts and covenants, carrying the durable quality of their prayer into promises and possessions.
terra: They stand by their testimonies, an enacted fidelity of witness immediately before their guarded prayer is restated.

luna: The section contrasts a showy prayer that is abandoned with sustained prayer; this ayah says they guard (يُحَافِظُونَ) their prayers, naming the continuation the image lacks. | terra: Guarding one's prayer supplies the second durable form named in the source section, opposed to possessing only its visible parts.

luna: In their own account of why they are in Saqar, they say they were not among those who prayed; it directly links denied dīn to prayer absent from life. | terra: The people of the Fire confess that they were not among those who prayed, beginning a compact reverse portrait of the practices in Surah 107.

luna: The next answer says they did not feed the poor; it supplies the same concrete failure to give that the section uses to expose the denier. | terra: They also did not feed the needy, joining failed prayer to failed care as the outward evidence of their condition.
terra: They joined those who treated serious things as play, adding a social performance that carried them away from the acts they named.

luna: They say they used to deny the Day of Recompense (يَوْمِ الدِّينِ); this directly names the denial whose practical signs the section traces through the orphan, poor and prayer. | terra: They finally confess that they denied the Day of Judgment; the sequence explicitly reads neglect of prayer and food as the lived form of تكذيب بالدين.
luna: This ayah says the person neither believed nor prayed; it is a direct opposite to 107's outward prayer that does not inhabit the prayer.

luna: The next ayah says he denied and turned away; beside 75:31 it supplies the explicit denial that the section depicts through deeds. | terra: He neither affirmed truth nor prayed, but denied and turned away; denial and abandoned prayer are placed in one bodily sequence.
terra: He then goes to his people swaggering, supplying a visible, audience-facing posture after the inward denial and failed prayer of 75:32.
luna: This adjacent passage begins by describing people who fulfill vows and fear a difficult day; it gives a sustained response to the source's promise that a beginning can fail to continue.

luna: The ayah describes feeding the orphan, poor person and captive, directly reversing the section's orphan-pushing and failure to urge food for the poor. | terra: The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, supplying the enacted care absent from the denier's life.

luna: They explain that they feed only for God's sake and seek neither reward nor thanks (لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ); the declared inward motive is the opposite of performing for an audience. | terra: They say they feed only for God's face and seek no reward or thanks from people, explicitly removing the spectator whose gaze sustains ostentatious action.
terra: The frown is itself a silent bodily statement, beginning a scene in which visible conduct toward a vulnerable seeker is judged.
terra: The triggering event is the blind man's arrival, making the response to one who cannot return the observer's gaze especially pertinent to audience-shaped behavior.
terra: Attention is directed toward the person who considers himself self-sufficient, identifying the socially impressive audience favored by the visible response.
terra: The Prophet gives that self-sufficient person attention, specifying the outward action that the passage corrects.
terra: The other man comes striving, a movement whose inward seriousness contrasts with the privileged audience's self-sufficiency.
terra: He comes in reverent fear, supplying the hidden quality beneath the unimpressive exterior.
terra: Attention is diverted from the striving, reverent man; the gaze and social audience visibly redirect the encounter.
terra: “Rather, you deny the Judgment” names the same object of denial; the following ayat answer it by placing every deed under observation.

luna: The ayah says guardians are appointed over people; it supplies the watching context for the source's idea that hidden intent and visible actions answer to judgment. | terra: Guardians stand over the deniers, relocating the decisive gaze from the human audience to witnesses who do not leave when spectators do.

luna: The next ayah describes those recorders as noble scribes; it specifies the record behind the judgment introduced in 82:10. | terra: The watchers are noble recorders, so no visible performance can define itself merely by how people read it.

luna: This ayah says the recorders know what people do; it directly joins inner accountability to the actual conduct that the section uses to expose denial. | terra: They know what people do, making deeds rather than surface profession the evidence attached to denial of Judgment in 82:9.
luna: The opening woe for those who give short measure introduces people whose outward exchange hides a deliberate shortfall, a concrete lie in action as the source's root ك ذ ب allows.
luna: This adjacent ayah says they take full measure from others, establishing the imbalance that makes their own short measure a false outward dealing.
luna: This adjacent ayah says that when they measure or weigh for others they give less; the action itself falls short of what the exchange appears to promise.
luna: The passage asks whether these short-measurers think they will be raised; it completes the connection between the deceptive act and the judgment denied in the section.
luna: This next ayah names the great Day on which they will be raised, completing the judgment scene introduced after the short measure.
luna: It says mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds; the specific dishonest measure is thus answerable to the judgment the section hears within دِين.
luna: After the short-measure passage, this ayah announces woe for deniers (لِلْمُكَذِّبِينَ); it names the falsehood behind the conduct rather than leaving it as a mere commercial mistake.

luna: The following ayah specifies that these deniers reject the Day of Recompense; this joins the conduct in 83:1–3 to the denied dīn in the source. | terra: The transgressors are identified as those who deny the Day of Judgment, and 83:14 then identifies what their own earning has done within.

luna: This ayah says their earnings have covered their hearts; that is a specific inward result of deeds covering what is beneath, completing the section's surface-and-interior image. | terra: What they earned has rusted over their hearts; repeated deeds become an actual covering on the interior, a dark counterpart to decorative paint on cloth.

luna: This ayah directly names failure to honor the orphan (لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ), the action by which the section says the denier of dīn is exposed. | terra: Failure to honor the orphan is presented as the concrete correction to a person's false reading of divine favor and humiliation.

luna: This ayah says they do not urge feeding the poor (وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ), matching the section's concrete measure of a life whose claim of religion is not carried into action. | terra: Failure to urge feeding the needy continues the behavioral evidence, closely matching the social proof attached to denial in Surah 107.
luna: The speaker boasts, “I have squandered abundant wealth” (أَهْلَكْتُ مَالًا لُّبَدًا); this gives a concrete public claim of spending whose real measure is tested by what follows.
luna: The next ayah asks whether he thinks no one sees him (أَن لَّمْ يَرَهُ أَحَدٌ); it puts the source's unseen intention and public appearance under God's gaze.
luna: After the boast of wealth, this ayah asks about the steep path; the following verses define what real, difficult giving entails, rather than treating a spending claim as enough.
luna: The first act on the steep path is freeing a person from bondage, a costly deed that contrasts with a merely impressive surface or claim.

luna: The next act is feeding during a day of hunger, directly opposing the section's failure to urge food for the poor. | terra: The difficult ascent includes feeding on a day of hunger, making costly continued action rather than a displayed gesture the measure.

luna: This ayah specifies feeding an orphan who is a relative (يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ), the direct opposite of pushing the orphan away. | terra: The recipient is an orphan of near relation, a direct enacted reversal of repelling the orphan.

luna: This ayah specifies feeding a needy person in severe poverty (مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ), making the section's withheld provision concrete. | terra: The same feeding reaches a destitute person in misery, completing the social act rather than withholding small aid.

luna: Belief is paired with urging one another to patience and compassion; this adds an enduring communal response to the feeding acts, unlike the section's halted care. | terra: Only then does the passage say the doer is among the believers who urge endurance and mercy, weaving creed, persistence, and action together.
luna: The next ayah identifies those who do these things as the companions of the right; their deeds, rather than a display, establish their standing.

luna: The source's root ك ذ ب describes falsehood that shows in conduct; this ayah opens the opposite path with a person who gives and is mindful of God, making generosity an enacted confirmation. | terra: The person who gives and is mindful begins the positive sequence whose sustained outcome is measured in the next ayat.

luna: The next ayah says this giver confirms the best; it supplies the truthful inward stance that the source contrasts with a life that only looks right. | terra: He confirms the best promise, وَصَدَّقَ بِٱلْحُسْنَىٰ, pairing truthful affirmation with the giving action of 92:5.

luna: This ayah says God will ease such a person toward ease, completing the sustained giving path that the source's interrupted-run idiom lacks. | terra: God eases the giver toward ease, so truthful action opens a course that continues rather than stopping after its first stride.

luna: The passage turns to the one who withholds and deems himself self-sufficient; this is the practical opposite of giving and encouragement to give in the section. | terra: The contrary person withholds and considers himself self-sufficient; the withheld act supplies the visible side of his denial.

luna: This ayah says the miser denies the good; the source's root ك ذ ب likewise connects denial to a visible life, and here denial is joined directly to withholding. | terra: He denies the best promise, وَكَذَّبَ بِٱلْحُسْنَىٰ, explicitly coupling تكذيب with the miserliness of 92:8.

luna: The next ayah says God will ease that person toward hardship, completing the consequence of the withholding-and-denial path. | terra: He is eased toward hardship, the terminal course corresponding to the denial and withholding that preceded it.

luna: The command not to oppress or repel the orphan (فَلَا تَقْهَرْ) directly reverses the section's image of pushing the orphan away. | terra: The command not to oppress the orphan is the direct behavioral reversal of pushing the orphan away.
luna: The next command not to rebuke the one who asks (فَلَا تَنْهَرْ) gives a concrete counterpart to the section's treatment of the vulnerable petitioner.
terra: أَرَءَيْتَ introduces the man who forbids, echoing 107:1's demand to look at a person whose conduct will disclose him.
terra: What he forbids is a servant praying, bringing prayer itself into the “have you seen?” exposure begun in 96:9.
terra: The question whether that praying servant stands on guidance asks the reader to judge beyond the forbidding man's visible authority.
terra: The servant may command reverence, supplying the action and stance that oppose the denier's coercive display.
terra: The persecutor denies and turns away, كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, joining the lie to its bodily movement.
terra: “Does he not know that God sees?” relocates the decisive gaze from human spectators to the One who sees the whole act and intent.

luna: The section says the painted exterior must answer to inward intention; this ayah joins prayer and almsgiving to making religion sincere for God (مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ), the opposite of an audience-facing surface. | terra: Prayer and almsgiving are commanded within مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ ٱلدِّينَ; sincere inward orientation makes the visible acts part of the fabric rather than paint on it.
luna: People emerge separately to be shown their deeds; this is a direct judgment scene for the source's claim that a life's acts expose the truth of its outward religious claim.
luna: The next ayah says whoever did an atom's weight of good will see it; it specifies that even a small real act is exposed.
luna: This ayah applies the same measure to an atom's weight of evil; it completes the source's image of deeds, rather than appearances, being answerable.

luna: The source's dictionary idiom describes an attack whose start may fail to continue; this ayah begins a sequence of steeds charging at speed, whose following actions carry the motion through rather than stopping. | terra: The panting chargers stage the animal run developed in the source dictionary; unlike the creature that stops to look behind, their motion is presented as sustained force.
luna: The next ayah has the steeds strike sparks as they run; this is the continuing force of the charge begun in 100:1.

luna: This ayah moves from the charge to a dawn raid, another step in the sustained attack opposite to a charge that peters out. | terra: The chargers make a dawn raid, carrying the run of 100:1 into its intended action rather than leaving it an impressive start.
luna: The steeds raise dust in their charge; this ayah contributes the continuing physical effect of motion before its completion in 100:5.

luna: The sequence ends with the steeds breaking into the midst of a group; this completes the attack that the source's negative idiom says may halt before its intended blow. | terra: They penetrate the center of the host, completing the charging movement and furnishing a concrete counter-image to the half-finished assault.
